'''''Araucaria angustifolia''''', the '''Paraná pine''', '''Brazilian pine''' or '''candelabra tree''',<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN |access-date=2 May 2026}}</ref> is a critically endangered species of [[conifer]] in the family [[Araucariaceae]]. Although the common names in various languages refer to the species as a [[pine]], it does not belong in the genus ''Pinus''.

==Description==
[[Image:Auraucaria angsmall1.jpg|thumb|left|285x285px|A very young ''A. angustifolia'']]

It is an [[evergreen]] tree usually growing to {{convert|40|m}} tall and {{convert|1|m|abbr=on}} [[diameter at breast height]]. The tree is fast growing; as much as {{convert|16|m|0|abbr=on|disp=or}} in 14 years in a [[Tree plantation|plantation]] at [[Puerto Piray]], Misiones Province, Argentina.<ref name="Wadsworth-1960">{{cite journal |last=Wadsworth |first=Frank H. |author2=(Chairman) |date=1960 |title=Records of forest plantation growth in Mexico, the West Indies, and Central and South America. Second annual report of the section on planting |journal=[[Caribbean Forester]] |publisher=Regional Committee on forest research, [[Latin American Forestry Commission]], [[Food and Agriculture Organization]], United Nations. |volume=21 |issue=Supplement |pages=272 + 16 pages refs |s2cid=127152584}} [[CAB Direct (database)|CABD]] [http://www.cabdirect.org/cabdirect/abstract/19600603436 19600603436].</ref>{{rp|13_8}} The leaves are thick, tough and scale like, triangular, {{convert|3|-|6|cm|abbr=on|frac=8}} long, {{convert|5|-|10|mm|frac=128}} broad at the base, and with razor-sharp edges and tip. They persist 10 to 15 years, so cover most of the tree except for the trunk and older branches.  The bark is uncommonly thick, up to 15 cm (6 in) deep.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Enright |first1=Neal J |title=Ecology of the Southern Conifers |last2=Hill |first2=Robert S. |date=1995 |publisher=Smithsonian Institution Press |location=Washington D.C. |page=124}}</ref> The inner bark and resin from the trunk of the tree is reddish.<ref name=":0" />

It is usually [[Plant reproductive morphology|dioecious]], with the male and female [[conifer cone|cones]] on separate trees, but occasionally there are also individuals who are [[Monoecy|monoecious]].<ref>[https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4210676/ Mating system of monoecious Araucaria angustifolia (Bert.) O. Kuntze, a predominately dioecious conifer species]</ref> The male (pollen) cones are oblong, {{convert|6|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}} long at first, expanding to {{convert|10|-|18|cm|0|abbr=on|frac=2}} long by {{convert|15|-|25|mm|frac=16|abbr=on}} broad at pollen release. Like all conifers it is wind pollinated. The female cones (seed), which mature in autumn about 18 months after pollination, are globose, large, {{convert|18|-|25|cm|0|abbr=on}} in diameter, and hold about 100–150 seeds. The cones disintegrate at maturity to release the approximately {{convert|5|cm|frac=2|abbr=on}} long [[nut (fruit)|nut]]-like seeds, which are then dispersed by animals, notably the [[Azure Jay|azure jay]], ''Cyanocorax caeruleus''.<ref name="f664">{{cite web| last=Vieira | first=Emerson Monteiro | title=Dispersão e predação de sementes da araucária (Araucaria angustifolia) Dispersal and predation of the Brazilian 'pine' (ARAUCARIA ANGUSTIFOLIA) seeds | website=ResearchGate | date=2009-07-01 | lang=pt | url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/310828471 | access-date=2025-06-08 | pages=85–95}}</ref>

===Similar species===
It can be distinguished from its close relative ''[[Araucaria araucana|A. araucana]]'' (found further southwest in South America), by its narrower leaves, seed with a much shorter bract scale, brown inner bark and white resin.<ref name=":0">{{cite book |last1=Farjon |first1=Aljos |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nqkKTQcGOtYC |title=A handbook of the world's conifers |date=2010 |publisher=Brill Publishers |isbn=978-90-04-17718-5 |location=Netherlands |page=188}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
The [[genus]] ''Araucaria'' was part of terrestrial flora since the [[Triassic]] and found its apogee in [[Gondwana]]. Today, it is restricted to the Southern Hemisphere and has 19 species.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.floresta.ufpr.br/pos-graduacao/defesas/pdf_dr/2009/t267_0296-D.pdf|title=ALEXANDRE BERNARDI KOEHLER|website=Floresta.ufpr.br|language=pt-BR|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121124020328/http://www.floresta.ufpr.br/pos-graduacao/defesas/pdf_dr/2009/t267_0296-D.pdf|archive-date=24 November 2012|access-date=19 July 2018}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Auraucaria angsmall3.jpg|thumb|left|''A. angustifolia'' in [[Campos do Jordão]]]]
[[File:Floresta Nacional de Caçador SC - Araucárias 6.jpg|thumb|left|Araucarias at ''Floresta Nacional de Caçador'', [[Santa Catarina (state)|Santa Catarina]], Brazil]]

The prehistoric distribution of ''A. angustifolia'' in earlier geologic periods was very different to the present day; fossils have been found in [[Northeast Region, Brazil|northeastern Brazil]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Instituto de Pesquisas e Estudos Florestais IPEF |url=https://www.ipef.br/identificacao/araucaria.angustifolia.asp}}</ref> The species moved into its present-day range in  [[South Region, Brazil|southern Brazil]] during the later [[Pleistocene]] and early [[Holocene]]. This [[chorology|chorological]] shift may possibly be due to [[Climate change (general concept)|climatic change]] and the migration of mountain flora by way of river courses.<ref>Müller-Starck, Gerhard & Schubert, Roland. [https://books.google.com/books?id=pdin2FGEHHoC&pg=PA94 ''Genetic response of forest systems to changing environmental conditions'']. Springer, 2001. p. 94</ref><ref>[http://amaivos.uol.com.br/amaivos09/noticia/noticia.asp?cod_noticia=7132&cod_canal=49 ''Registros históricos da Araucária - Entrevista com Hermann Behling''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131029201628/http://amaivos.uol.com.br/amaivos09/noticia/noticia.asp?cod_noticia=7132&cod_canal=49|date=2013-10-29}}. Unisinos. Disponível em Amaivos, acesso 24 fev 2011</ref> Around 149,000 years ago, the species’ distribution became divided into two separate Brazilian populations: one in [[Mantiqueira Mountains|Serra da Mantiqueira]], which is smaller but exhibits higher genetic diversity, and another on the southern plateau, which underwent a range expansion around 4000 years ago, possibly associated with human activity.<ref>[https://agencia.fapesp.br/dispersal-of-araucaria-trees-in-atlantic-rainforest-was-influenced-by-pre-columbian-people/31200 Dispersal of Araucaria trees in Atlantic Rainforest was influenced by pre-Columbian people]</ref><ref>[https://nsojournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ecog.06756 Evaluating the impact of historical climate and early human groups in the Araucaria Forest of eastern South America]</ref> Covering an original area of {{convert|233000|km2}},<ref name="Silva">{{cite journal|url=http://www.cnpf.embrapa.br/publica/boletim/boletarqv/boletim43/silva.pdf|author1=Helton Damin da Silva |author2=Antonio F. Jurado Bellote |author3=Carlos Alberto Ferreira |author4=Itamar Antonio Bognola |year=2001 |title=Recomendação de solos para ''Araucaria angustifolia'' com base nas suas propriedades físicas e químicas |journal=Boletim de Pesquisa Florestal |volume=43 |pages=61–74 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070609125453/http://www.cnpf.embrapa.br/publica/boletim/boletarqv/boletim43/silva.pdf |archive-date=2007-06-09 }}</ref> it has now lost an estimated 97% of its habitat to logging, agriculture, and [[silviculture]].<ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" />

Besides southern Brazil, it is also found in high-altitude areas of southern [[Minas Gerais]], in central [[Rio de Janeiro]] and in the east and south of [[São Paulo (state)|São Paulo]], but more typically in the states of [[Paraná (state)|Paraná]], [[Santa Catarina (state)|Santa Catarina]] and [[Rio Grande do Sul]]. According to a study made by Brazilian researcher [[Reinhard Maack]], the original area of occurrence represented 36.67% of the Paraná state ({{convert|73088|km2|disp=or|abbr=on}}), 60.13% of the Santa Catarina state ({{convert|57332|km2|disp=or|abbr=on}}), 21.6% of the São Paulo state ({{convert|53613|km2|disp=or|abbr=on}}) and 17.38% of the Rio Grande do Sul state ({{convert|48968|km2|disp=or|abbr=on}}).<ref name="Silva" /> It is also found in the northeast of [[Argentina]] ([[Misiones Province|Misiones]] and [[Corrientes Province|Corrientes]]), locally in [[Paraguay]] ([[Alto Paraná Department|Alto Paraná]]), growing in low mountains at altitudes of {{convert|500|-|1800|m}} and in northern regions of [[Uruguay]] where it was thought to be extinct until recent discoveries.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Arballo|first=Eduardo|title=Caracterización de los bosques nativos uruguayos según sus aves|url=http://www.guayubira.org.uy/monte/seminario/ponencias/Arballo.pdf|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210626162725/http://www.guayubira.org.uy/monte/seminario/ponencias/Arballo.pdf|archive-date=2021-06-26|access-date=2019-01-16|website=www.guayubira.org.uy}}</ref>

It prefers well drained, slightly [[acidic soil]] but will tolerate almost any soil type provided drainage is good. It requires a subtropical/temperate climate with abundant rainfall, tolerating occasional frosts down to about {{convert|-5|to|-20|C|F}}.{{cn|date=December 2025}}

==Ecology==
[[Image:Araucaria angustifolia en Uruguay.jpg|thumb|180x180px|''Araucaria angustifolia'' in [[Cerro Largo Department|Cerro Largo]], Uruguay]]The seeds are very important for the native animals. Several mammals and birds eat the {{lang|pt|pinhão}}, and it has an important ecological role in [[Araucaria moist forests]] (a sub-type of the Brazilian [[Atlantic Forest]]).{{citation needed|date=March 2023}}

In a long term study observing the feeding behaviour throughout the year of the squirrel [[Sciurus ingrami|''Guerlinguetus brasiliensis ingrami'']] in a secondary ''A. angustifolia'' forest in the Parque Recreativo Primavera in the vicinity of the city of [[Curitiba]], Paraná, of the ten plant species of which the squirrel ate the seeds or nuts, seeds of ''A. angustifolia'' were the most important food item in the fall, with a significant percentage of their diet in the winter consisting of the seeds as well.

The squirrels cache seeds, but it is unclear how this affects recruitment.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bordignon |first1=Marcelo |last2=Monteiro-Filho |first2=E. L. A. |date=1999 |title=Seasonal Food Resources of the Squirrel ''Sciurus ingrami'' in a Secondary ''Araucaria'' Forest in Southern Brazil |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/233029598 |journal=Studies on Neotropical Fauna and Environment |volume=34 |issue=3 |pages=137–140 |doi=10.1076/snfe.34.3.137.8910 |bibcode=1999SNFE...34..137B |access-date=15 October 2018}}</ref>

== Conservation ==
According to one calculation it has lost an estimated 97% of its habitat to logging, agriculture, and silviculture in the last century.<ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" /> People also eat the seeds, which may reduce recruitment.<ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" /> It was therefore listed by the IUCN as 'vulnerable in 1998 and 'critically endangered' in 2008.<ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" />

== Uses ==
{{broader|Araucaria#Uses}}
[[File:Pinhas.jpg|thumb|''Araucaria angustifolia'' cones ({{lang|pt|pinhas}}) and nuts ({{lang|pt|pinhões}})]]
[[File:Male cones of Araucaria angustifolia.jpg|thumb|Dry male cones|alt=Two dry male cones lie side by side on a table|217x217px]]
''Araucaria angustifolia'' is a popular garden tree in subtropical areas, planted for its unusual effect of the thick, 'reptilian' branches with a very symmetrical appearance.{{citation needed|date=March 2023}}

The seeds of ''A. angustifolia'', similar to large [[pine nut]]s, are edible, and are extensively harvested in southern Brazil (Paraná, Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul states), an occupation particularly important for the region's small population of [[Indigenous peoples in Brazil|natives]] (the [[Kaingáng]] and other [[Jê languages|Southern Jê]]). The seeds, called {{lang|pt|pinhão}} {{IPA|pt|piˈɲɐ̃w|}} are popular as a winter snack. The city of [[Lages]], in Santa Catarina, holds a popular {{lang|pt|pinhão}} fair, in which mulled wine and boiled ''Araucaria'' seeds are consumed. {{convert|3400|t|lb}} of seeds are collected annually in Brazil.

It is also used as a [[softwood]] timber in stair treads and [[Woodworking joints|joinery]].<ref>{{cite web|last1=Buckley|first1=Michael|title=A basic guide to softwoods and hardwoods|url=http://www.worldhardwoods.com/files/articles_basicguide.pdf|publisher=worldhardwoods.com|date=2005|access-date=1 October 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190819093840/http://www.worldhardwoods.com/files/articles_basicguide.pdf|archive-date=19 August 2019}}</ref> The species is widely used in [[folk medicine]].<ref>{{cite journal |author=A. M. Freitas |author2=M. T. R. Almeida |author3=C. R. Andrighetti-Fröhner|author4=F. T. G. S. Cardozo |author5=C. R. M. Barardi|author6=M. R. Farias |author7=C. M. O. Simões |name-list-style=amp|year=2009 |title=Antiviral activity-guided fractionation from ''Araucaria angustifolia'' leaves extract |journal=[[Journal of Ethnopharmacology]] |volume=126 |issue=3 |pages=512–517 |pmid=19761825 |doi=10.1016/j.jep.2009.09.005|doi-access=free }}</ref>

While ''A. angustifolia'' is a main species and dominant in South Brazil, it's also grown as an ornamental plant in parks of towns and cities of Chile, from [[Santiago]] to [[Valdivia]]. It grows better in low altitudes than the local ''Araucaria araucana'', hence its use as a substitute in the [[Chilean Central Valley|Central Valley]] and coastal regions of Chile.<ref name="Tom2018">{{Cite web|url=https://treesandshrubsonline.org/articles/araucaria/araucaria-angustifolia-x-araucana/|title=Araucaria angustifolia × araucana|access-date=2021-04-22|website=Trees and Shrubs Online|last=Christian|first=Tom|url-status=live|publisher=[[International Dendrology Society]]|year=2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200814165622/https://treesandshrubsonline.org/articles/araucaria/araucaria-angustifolia-x-araucana/ |archive-date=2020-08-14 }}</ref> In some places like the town of [[Melipeuco]] ''A. angustifolia'' can be seen growing side by side with ''A. araucana''.<ref name="Tom2018" />

The hybrid ''Araucaria angustifolia × araucana'' is thought to have first arisen "in a plantation forestry environment in Argentina sometime in the late 19th or early 20th century".<ref name=Tom2018/> It is thus not a natural hybrid as there are more than 1000 km between the natural stands of the two species.<ref name=Tom2018/>
